sections.markdown:
## C — Driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs: alcohol and drug impairment, how alcohol affects driving skills, standard drinks and alcohol concentration, lower-risk choices, the DWI law and implied consent, penalties by offense, ignition interlock, felony DWI, the underage no-tolerance rule, commercial drivers, cannabis and open containers
Knowledge domain: why impaired driving is illegal and deadly in Minnesota, how alcohol and drugs affect driving, how alcohol concentration rises and falls, the legal limits and testing duties, the penalties for each offense, the rules for drivers under twenty-one and commercial drivers, and the cannabis and open container laws.

FACT_ID: sec14-F01 | anchor: A01
It is illegal to drive on Minnesota roads while impaired by alcohol or any other substance. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec14-F02 | anchor: A01
In alcohol-related crashes the impaired driver is the one most often killed, and young men are more likely than others to drive impaired. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec14-F03 | anchor: A01
Minnesota law bans driving while impaired by controlled or intoxicating substances, which include illegal drugs, prescription and over-the-counter drugs such as cold medicines, and household products. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec14-F04 | anchor: A01
A legal drug that does not impair you alone can have a powerful intoxicating effect when mixed with alcohol, so the safest rule is not to mix drugs with driving at all. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec14-F05 | anchor: A01
You may possess and use a prescribed drug if your doctor tells you it will not affect your ability to drive safely, and you should follow warning labels and the doctor's orders. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec14-F06 | anchor: A01
Never use a drug to hide fatigue; the only cure for being tired is rest. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec14-F07 | anchor: A01
Alcohol is a depressant, the amount in your blood is called the alcohol concentration, and your driving ability is impaired after just one drink. [A01]
Why it matters: impairment after one drink is a classic test item.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec14-F08 | anchor: A01
Alcohol makes you misjudge how impaired you are, so you may speed, misjudge stopping distances, skip your seat belt and stop driving defensively. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec14-F09 | anchor: A01
Alcohol narrows the range of eye movement and reduces peripheral vision, and high alcohol concentrations can blur vision. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec14-F10 | anchor: A02
Alcohol slows reaction time, makes drivers over-steer and weave, dulls perception of sights and sounds, and weakens coordination, balance and attention. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec14-F11 | anchor: A02
About the same amount of alcohol is usually found in a 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, a 9-ounce wine cooler and a typical mixed drink. [A02]
Why it matters: standard drink sizes are a likely numeric item.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec14-F12 | anchor: A02
Mixed drinks may hold more than the standard 1.5 ounces of alcohol, and the alcohol content of beers can vary by as much as 40 percent. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec14-F13 | anchor: A02
A drink's proof is twice its alcohol percentage, so 80-proof whiskey is 40 percent alcohol. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec14-F14 | anchor: A02
Drinking more than one standard drink per hour raises your alcohol concentration. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec14-F15 | anchor: A02
The only way to lower your alcohol concentration is to wait, since the body generally clears about one drink per hour and coffee, exercise or cold showers do not speed it up. [A02]
Why it matters: coffee does not sober you up is a classic test item.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec14-F16 | anchor: A02
Someone with a higher share of body fat than another person of the same weight reaches a higher alcohol concentration from the same amount of alcohol. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec14-F17 | anchor: A03
The safest policy is simple: if you will drink, do not drive, and if you will drive, do not drink, and make your plan while you are still sober. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec14-F18 | anchor: A03
A person in control of a moving or parked vehicle with an alcohol concentration of 0.08 percent or higher, or 0.04 percent in a commercial vehicle, can be arrested for DWI. [A03]
Why it matters: the legal limits are among the most tested numbers in the manual.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec14-F19 | anchor: A03
Even at 0.04 percent a driver can face DWI arrest when an officer can prove alcohol caused the driving errors. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec14-F20 | anchor: A03
Under the implied consent law, if an officer has probable cause to believe you are impaired while driving or in physical control of a vehicle, you must take a blood, breath or urine test, and refusing is a crime. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec14-F21 | anchor: A03
Refusing the implied consent test leads to a revocation lasting from one to six years, with the length set by how many offenses are already on your record. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec14-F22 | anchor: A03
A roadside preliminary breath test only indicates your alcohol level and has limited use as court evidence, while the blood, breath or urine test required after arrest can be used as evidence. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec14-F23 | anchor: A04
An alcohol-related revocation brings a $680 reinstatement fee, a new license application and possibly enrollment in the Ignition Interlock Device Program. [A04]
Why it matters: the reinstatement fee is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec14-F24 | anchor: A04
Penalties are harsher with prior DWI arrests, an alcohol concentration of 0.16 percent or more, a child under 16 in the vehicle, a driver under 21, or a refused preliminary breath test. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec14-F25 | anchor: A04
A driver found at 0.08 percent or more, or who refuses testing, may get a seven-day temporary license, after which the license is revoked. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec14-F26 | anchor: A04
A first offense brings at least a 90-day revocation, or 30 days with a guilty plea to DWI, and a penalty listed as 90 days in jail, a $1,000 fine or both. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec14-F27 | anchor: A04
After a first offense no work permit is issued until 15 days of revocation have passed and reinstatement requirements are met, and none at all if the alcohol concentration was 0.16 percent or more. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec14-F28 | anchor: A04
A second offense within 10 years of the first brings at least a one-year revocation, a penalty listed as one year in jail, a $3,000 fine or both, and impounded license plates. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec14-F29 | anchor: A04
A third offense within 10 years brings at least three years without a license, cancellation, a chemical use assessment, required ignition interlock, and a forfeited vehicle with impounded plates. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec14-F30 | anchor: A05
An ignition interlock device on the vehicle's starter will not let the vehicle start if your breath shows an alcohol concentration of 0.02 percent or more. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec14-F31 | anchor: A05
Drivers whose licenses are canceled and denied as inimical to public safety must use the ignition interlock for three to six years to regain full privileges. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec14-F32 | anchor: A05
A fourth DWI arrest within 10 years, a prior felony DWI conviction, or a criminal vehicular homicide conviction while impaired can lead to a felony DWI charge. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec14-F33 | anchor: A05
A felony DWI can be punished by as much as seven years in prison, followed by five years of conditional release, and a $14,000 fine. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec14-F34 | anchor: A05
A driver under 21 may not drive with any detectable alcohol, and a conviction brings a 30-day suspension, or 180 days for a second conviction. [A05]
Why it matters: the no-tolerance rule is a likely test item for teens.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec14-F35 | anchor: A05
A commercial driver loses the commercial license for at least one year on a first offense such as driving a commercial vehicle at 0.04 or more, and a detectable level below 0.04 means 24 hours out of service. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec14-F36 | anchor: A06
Driving under the influence of cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, hemp-derived products, artificially derived cannabinoids or THC is illegal. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec14-F37 | anchor: A06
Using cannabis flower or any cannabis or hemp-derived product in a vehicle on a street or highway is illegal. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec14-F38 | anchor: A06
Opened or partly emptied cannabis or hemp-derived products must ride in the trunk, or in an area not normally occupied if there is no trunk, never in the glove or utility compartment. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec14-F39 | anchor: A06
You may not drink or have an open alcoholic beverage container inside a vehicle on a public street or highway, and you may not allow passengers to do so either. [A06]
Why it matters: open container rules cover passengers too.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec14-F40 | anchor: A06
Using, possessing or selling controlled substances in a motor vehicle is prohibited. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0099]

Misconceptions: coffee, exercise and cold showers do not lower alcohol concentration; legal prescription or cold medicines can still be illegal to drive on when they impair you; you can be arrested below the general limit if alcohol caused your errors; refusing a test is a crime, not a way out; under twenty-one there is no safe amount.
Mnemonics: point zero eight for drivers, point zero four for commercial, point zero two locks the interlock, any amount under twenty-one; one drink per hour out; proof is double the percent.
Glossary: alcohol concentration means the amount of alcohol in the blood; DWI means driving while impaired; implied consent means the duty to take a chemical test when an officer has probable cause; preliminary screening test means the roadside breath test used before arrest; ignition interlock device means a breath tester wired to the starter; inimical to public safety means the denial status under which drivers with canceled licenses must use the ignition interlock for three to six years.
Dynamic facts: the reinstatement fee, fines and penalty periods are set by law and can change, and the statewide alcohol crash statistics on the first page of the chapter change each year; recheck them against an official DPS source before each release.
